messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Ravi

Ravi was thirty-two when the chest pain began—a tightness that started one morning as he sat at his desk designing an interface for a healthcare app. He'd dismissed it at first, attributed it to stress, to the coffee, to posture. But within hours he was in an emergency room, and within days he learned he had myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle that could have killed him. The doctors were careful with their language, spoke of "lucky timing" and "early intervention," but what Ravi heard was that his body had betrayed him without warning, that something fundamental inside him was damaged, that death had come close enough to brush against him in the fluorescent light of an ambulance bay.

Three years later, Ravi found himself unable to return to that proximity. Hospitals became places he could not enter—not to visit a colleague, not to accompany his wife for a routine scan. The sight of an ambulance on the freeway would send his stomach into a knot so tight he had to pull over. When his cardiologist requested he come in for his annual check-up, Ravi cancelled twice, then a third time. His wife, Priya, had stopped asking about the appointments. She'd learned that each time she mentioned the word "examination," Ravi's jaw would clench, and he would find reasons to leave the room. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally broken, that the illness had exposed something defective in him that no amount of reassurance could fix. His weakness had been made visible once, and he was certain it would be again—perhaps more catastrophically. This conviction, that he was a weak person at his core, had become the lens through which he interpreted every physical sensation. When his heart raced during a meeting, it was not anxiety; it was proof of his defectiveness. When he felt emotionally flat, unable to summon enthusiasm even for things he once loved, he took it as confirmation that something essential in him had died along with the threat.

The threat monitoring had become relentless. Any delay—a text message that took an hour to answer, a meeting that ran long, a traffic jam—triggered a cascade of catastrophic thinking. His mind would race: something bad is happening, someone is hurt, time is running out. He was certain that safety was a fiction others told themselves, a comfortable lie. Even when Priya held his hand and told him he was fine, that his recent test results were normal, that he was safe, Ravi could not believe her. His body would not believe her. His muscles remained constantly tense, coiled as if ready to flee from an invisible threat. He had become hypervigilant to every internal sensation—a skipped heartbeat, a moment of lightheadedness—and each one felt like evidence that disaster was imminent, that the illness was returning, that his body was still betraying him.

This vigilance had driven him deeper into avoidance. He stopped going to the gym because exercise felt dangerous, a way of stressing his compromised body. He declined social invitations that might involve walking long distances or situations where he couldn't easily access help. At work, he'd shifted away from projects involving healthcare clients, which meant turning down promotions and high-visibility work. His manager had begun to notice his withdrawal, the way he seemed distracted, the projects he was avoiding. What Ravi didn't tell anyone was that each time he avoided something—each cancelled appointment, each declined invitation—the threat felt more real, more pressing. The avoidance itself became evidence that danger was real, that his fear was justified. His body remained on high alert, and his mind continued to spin stories about his weakness, his defectiveness, his inability to trust his own safety. The cycle had tightened around him so completely that he could no longer see a way out. It was only when Priya, after a particularly difficult evening where Ravi had become inconsolable over a delayed lab result, insisted that he see a therapist that he finally agreed. He came to the first session exhausted, convinced that nothing could help, but also—beneath the numbness and the fear—desperate for someone to tell him that he wasn't as broken as he believed.
